b: This Book Week, let’s celebrate the power of reading (not just the costumes) By Tracey Cheung — August 21, 2023, 11.25am It’s officially that time of year when parents scour the shops for the perfect Book Week costume. For some, making sure their little one looks just like their chosen storybook character involves face-painting, finding the right glasses, hat, bow or cape — sometimes tail and ears. Among all this, it can be easy to lose the true meaning behind Book Week. Wendy Rapee, chair of Children’s Book Council of Australia, says the event is an opportunity to draw attention to the joy of reading and for advocating for stories in children’s lives. Rapee explains this is the reason behind this year’s CBCA Children’s Book Week theme: Read, Inspire, Grow . “Like dressing up, reading books presents the opportunity to walk in someone else’s shoes, to experience adventures, feel things they have never felt and hopefully learn something about the world they live in,” says Rapee. Over the years, I have found that reading stories to my daughter has helped me teach her helpful life skills and ways of thinking. And I’m not the only one with this experience. Sue Cahill, a student wellbeing leader at St Charles Borromeo Primary School in Melbourne, says she finds storybooks extremely powerful in teaching her school children how to deal with various issues, such as school refusal, friendships and bullying. She used the book I Am Jack by Susanne Gervay to help two boys in a bullying si

Learning valuable relationship skills Venita Dimos is a lawyer, mediator and the author of children’s book series Mini and Milo . Each book in the series has a different theme, including mindset, communication and listening. As a lawyer and mediator, Dimos has witnessed the profound impact of unresolved conflict in families and workplaces. Her series was driven by a heartfelt need to teach children key relationship skills early on in life. “Managing conflict is not a skill you are born with – it’s a skill you need to learn,” she says. “Unfortunately, most people don’t learn this in early childhood, so grow up learning on the job with their relationships at stake.” Recently, I read Dimos’ Mini and Milo: The Teeny-Tiny Voice . At the time, my daughter had picked up a swear word from somewhere. When I told her to stop saying it, she said to me, “I want to stop but the voice inside my head keeps telling me to say it.” The book taught her that we have greater power over our thoughts than we think, which eventually helped her to stop swearing.

Discussion of sensitive topics Books have also helped encourage conversations with my daughter about issues I have otherwise felt unsure about how to open myself. For example, while I found it awkward to start conversations about the topic of body safety, reading My Body! What I Say Goes! by Jayneen Sanders helped break the ice. Lucy Kippist, 44, a community manager of Mums & Co and mother of two from Sydney, found books helpful when helping her children get through the grief of losing their grandparents. She says How Can I Help Papa? A Child’s Journey Through Loss and Healing by Elissa Al-Chokhachy helped give her children new words to describe their feelings around grief. While reading, they learned that part of grieving someone you loved is to remember the happy times. “It elicited some happy memories with their grandfather. We talked about the more fun things, like how he used to do Lego with them,” says Kippist. Alyson Simpson, a professor of English and literacy education at the University of Sydney, says parents don’t need to expect that a reading session will be a literacy lesson. “Allow children to explore the books,” she says. “My grandson finds more things in the pictures than I do sometimes.”

Fostering friendships Elisha Casagrande, 35, found that her son was able to find a message in a book without any prompts from her. The Brisbane-based health coach recently started home-schooling her son, who was having trouble being apart from his friends, so she decided to read The Giving Tree by Shel Silverstein to him. In the book, a boy makes brief visits to a ’living” tree several times over the years, until he becomes an old man. “My son picked up that relationships can still last, provided there’s some connection over time, like the man who kept connecting with that tree,” says Casagrande. When I asked my 5-year-old daughter who she was going to dress up as for her first Book Week, it was an easy choice: Cinderella. Although I know she is drawn to the story because of the pretty princess, after reading the book together, I also know she understands the morals behind the story, such as the importance of kindness.

b: Don’t ask me to give the Queen a minute’s silence, ask me for the truth about British colonialism By Lidia Thorpe Wednesday, 14 September 2022 — 12.07 AEST ’We’re not grieving a singular human life, we’re reeling from the violence that is the legacy of the monarchy.” — Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP News of the Queen’s death broke on the same day as my cousin’s funeral. Exam Format The VCE English exam is a three-hour exam, plus 15 minutes of reading time. It has three sections, and you are required to complete all three sections. Each section is worth the same number of marks, so you should spend the same amount of time on each.
Exam Specifications

Overall Conditions The examination will be sat at a time and date to be set annually by the Victorian Curriculum and Assessment Authority (VCAA). VCAA examination rules will apply. There will be 15 minutes of reading time and 3 hours of writing time. The examination will be assessed by a panel appointed by the VCAA. The examination will contribute 50 per cent to the study score.

Format The Task Book will be sixteen pages in length. The front page contains the general cover notes and instructions, including rules about what you can and can’t take into the exam. An English and/or bilingual printed dictionary is permitted. Mobile Phones and/pr any unauthrosied electronic devices are not permitted.
Exam Mindset, Timing and FAQs

How Your Paper Is Marked Each section is marked by at least two assessors, each giving a score out of 10, combined into a mark out of 20. If the two scores are too far apart, a third (or further) assessor reads the response. Assessors mark holistically against the expected qualities, and always in relation to the topic or title. They read every word and reward as far as they can. In 2025 the average for each section sat around 5.4 to 5.5 out of 10.

Attitude Is a Predictor An Australian study of students under test conditions, controlling for ability, found that attitude alone predicted results. “Confident striders” (prepared, and trusting that the test would be fair) did best; students who expected the test to be unfair and stressful tended to fulfil that prophecy. Practical takeaways: Trust the paper to be fair. Recent papers have been. A question may be phrased unexpectedly, but you are transferring skills you have practised to a new instance. A little nerves is useful. Adrenaline speeds thinking. Worrying about things you cannot control only takes up brain space. Confidence comes from preparation , not from hoping.

Habits of Successful Students Train for three hours. Do some study in three-hour blocks so the exam is not the first time you concentrate that long. Work out what breakfast keeps you going. Practise, get feedback, act on it, practise again. Eat well, sleep, and exercise to burn off anxiety when it tips from useful to unhelpful. Have a backup plan. No single exam decides your future. Missing a first-choice course often means a transfer a year later.

Time Discipline The three sections are worth equal marks, so give each one hour. The first marks in any response are the easiest to earn. An extra half hour polishing one essay gains far less than the same half hour spent on the next. Use the room clock, and when the hour is up, move on.

Plan, Then Write Planning is not extra work; it shifts the work. When you write without a plan, you are deciding what to say and how to say it at the same time, and your brain switches between the two and loses time. Plan first (only you need to read it), check it is relevant to the topic, then give your full attention to expression. Fluency is assessed in every section.

Frequently Asked Questions How many quotes should I use in Section A? There is no number. It depends on how many other kinds of evidence you use (structure, character, setting, language features, context), and every quote must be explained, not just included. Should I memorise a strong practice response? No, in any section. You cannot know the topic, title or text, and a memorised piece that does not answer the question cannot score highly. Which section should I do first? Personal choice. Some students do A, B, C in order; others start with whichever they plan fastest. Try different orders in practice exams. What should I do the night before? Put the books away and sleep. A year of preparation will not be changed by two more hours. What if I make a mistake? Cross it out neatly and keep going. If you realise mid-essay you have drifted, fix your topic sentences, but stay within your hour. Checking your plan early is the best prevention. What if I don’t get the score I want? You get the score you get. It is a snapshot of one day, and your skills keep growing after it.
Strategies for Addressing the Requirements

Section A In Section A you will write an essay that responds to one of the two given topics on a text you have studied. You can choose to write on either your Unit 1 text or your Unit 4 text. In your answer book you will need to identify the text on which you are writing and the topic (i or ii) you are responding to by shading the relevant box. Spend a few minutes unpacking the topic you feel most comfortable responding to. Look carefully at each term in the topic and make sure you understand its meaning and significance. Use the strategies for identifying topic words, direction words and limiting words outlined on pages 48–50 in English Year 12. Spend about 5 minutes writing a brief plan that includes your contention, three or four topic sentences and one or two pieces of textual evidence for each topic sentence. The following strategies will help you to address the Section A requirements and criteria. Address the topic in full. Strong responses take account of every word in the topic, including the limiting words, rather than writing about one key term in a general way. Use your dictionary. Make sure you understand the meanings of all the words in the topic. Your dictionary will also give you some synonyms for key terms in the topic, and using these will give your writing more variety and precision. Consider a range of textual features. Don’t limit your reasons and evidence to just what the characters say and do. While authors do use characters to explore ideas, they also u

Section B In Section B you will write a text that responds to a given title and at least one piece of stimulus material. In the answer book, you will need to shade the box of your chosen Framework, and the box (or boxes) corresponding to the stimulus (or stimuli) you have responded to. The following strategies will help you to address the Section B criteria and weave the stimuli and title into your creative piece. Ensure your writing is clearly relevant to your chosen Framework. This involves integrating concepts and perspectives that you’ve explored during the year. When you are revising in preparation for the exam, refer to your notes and written pieces to stay aligned with the core ideas of the Framework. Integrate the title and at least one stimulus into your writing. You must use at least one of the stimuli. The stimulus should not just be referenced superficially; it should be woven into the fabric of your piece. This could mean, for example, using a text stimulus as the basis for a central idea; using a text stimulus as a direct quote at a key point in your text; or drawing inspiration from a visual stimulus to set a scene. Similarly, the title provided for your Framework should provide an idea, a character arc, a central image or another key element of your writing. Give your piece cohesion and structure. Section C In Section C you will analyse a text in which the writer seeks to persuade a particular audience to agree with their point of view on an issue. t: How the Marker Reads Your Essay
b: How the Marker Reads Your Essay Examiners do not read your essay the way a friendly teacher does – they read it in passes, testing it against the criteria. Knowing the passes lets you write for them.

The Six Passes First, the scope audit: the topic is broken into its explicit and implicit parts, including modifying words (“unrelenting cruelty”, not just “cruelty”) and both halves of a double-barrelled prompt. A dimension you never address keeps you out of the 8–10 range. Second, the summary filter: every sentence is silently sorted into retelling, explaining, or analysing how the author constructs meaning – and if retelling dominates, the essay cannot reach the upper band no matter how fluent it is. Third, the topic-sentence thread: conceptual topic sentences that build a progressive argument separate 9–10 essays from 7–8 essays that give three parallel examples of one idea. Fourth, the authorial hand: markers look for sentences whose subject is the author (“Harrison constructs…”, “Wilder juxtaposes…”) – writing about characters as though they are real people is a mid-band signature. Fifth, evidence gravity: quotes that stand alone as their own sentences read mid-band; short quotes woven into your own grammar, drawn from across the whole text, read upper-band. Sixth, the gap analysis: the difference between your mark and the next band is always something specific and nameable – which is why good feedback tells you what was missing, not just what was there.

What the Bands Feel Like A 5 is relevant but basic: simple structure, simple vocabulary, evidence that supports plot points. A 7 is clear and detailed, uses evidence effectively, but stays at the level of what the text shows rather than how and why it was built that way. A 9 or 10 is sophisticated and perceptive: it reframes the topic conceptually, treats the text as a construction, uses precise metalanguage correctly, and integrates evidence so smoothly the quotation marks could be removed without breaking the sentence.

Section-Specific Traps In Section A, a contention that simply agrees or disagrees without a bigger conceptual claim caps the essay in the middle band, and ignoring the text’s social and historical values keeps the top band out of reach. In Section B, a competent story that never engages the Framework’s ideas sits mid-band, as do clichéd premises and unearned endings – while adapted echoes of your mentor texts signal studied craft. In Section C, “the readers” is a mid-band audience; the upper band names who the writer targets and what they are being positioned to think, feel and do. Naming a technique without explaining its function for that specific audience is label-picking, and it caps the analysis no matter how many techniques you spot. Track the argument’s arc and tonal shifts; treat any visual as part of the argument, not a separate exhibit.

The three EQs are interconnected: the quality of your ideas (EQ1) sets the level of challenge for structuring and substantiating them (EQ2), and language (EQ3) is judged by how well it communicates those ideas. b: Part 12 Section A: Analytical Response to a Text The 2025 topics were deliberately narrow — specified ideas and values rather than broad prompts — and this shaped how responses needed to be structured, sequenced and evidenced. Students with topic-interpretation strategies handled both familiar and unfamiliar phrasings well. Topic types Propositional topics offered a proposition with a command term: Discuss , Do you agree? or To what extent do you agree? You may challenge the proposition where warranted, but never the topic's conceptual focus itself — a topic linking love and destruction requires discussing both, though "inseparable" can be contested. Quotation topics paired a quotation with a proposition. There was no obligatory way to use the quotation, but how you used it revealed your understanding of what it conveys in context. The verbs The verb in a topic carries the author's purpose, and flattening every verb into a generic "presents" was unwise. Assessors also warned that verbs are often nominalised or implied, and new ones appear each year. Used in 2025 New in 2025 celebrates, challenges, condemns, demonstrates, displays, explores, highlights, mocks, shows, suggests is (a cry for), depicts, glorifies, warns Implications: where the top marks lived There was a direct correlation between recognising a topic's implications and higher scores. b: Part 12 Section C: Analysis of Argument and Language The 2025 text was a letter to a community newsletter from a "local resident" proposing that a regional town replace its annual fireworks with an alternative celebration. Students found it highly accessible — which made the discriminators sharper. Background information is not decoration The publication details and the author's "local resident" persona had to be used: inferring the regional audience and its values, the author's altruistic credibility, and the unhurried "evolution, not urgency" framing enabled the most focused analyses. Read the background inferentially before writing — the analysis flows from it. The argument structure most students saw Establishing a shared value: love of the celebration in its beautiful setting. Before the exam Build a topic-interpretation routine: identify the conceptual focus, the command term, the verb, and at least two implications before planning. Rehearse unfamiliar-verb strategy — and pack a dictionary. Practise writing to a fixed title in Section B without bending a pre-prepared piece to fit. For Section C practice, always start from the background information and write down audience, purpose and author positioning before analysing. Section A: open and close each paragraph with sentences that link your ideas to the topic; use the conclusion to resolve the question. Assess your current study habits

Identifying strengths and weaknesses Take a few minutes to jot down what’s working well in your current study routine. What areas could use some improvement? Consider factors like time management, focus, and understanding of different subjects.

Setting realistic goals Based on your assessment, you could start by setting 2-3 specific, achievable goals for improving your study habits. Make these goals SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. Write them down and place them somewhere visible as a daily reminder.

Create a personalised study schedule Now that you know where you stand, it’s time to map out a path to exam success. Think of your study schedule as a roadmap to help you navigate your way through VCE studies.

Time management tips List all your subjects and the topics you need to cover for each. Assess how much time you have until your exams. Consider prioritising subjects based on difficulty and your current performance. Using a study schedule template Remember: Be realistic with your schedule. If you’re not a morning person, a sunrise study session may not suit you. Try to work with your natural rhythms, and not against them.

t: Find a study schedule template that works for you – digital or physical, whichever works best.
b: Find a study schedule template that works for you – digital or physical, whichever works best. Block out fixed commitments like school, extracurriculars, and family time. Allocate study blocks for each subject, ensuring a mix of subjects each day. Don’t forget to schedule breaks and ’me time’ to avoid feelings of burnout.
Organise your study materials A cluttered space can contribute to a cluttered mind. Here are some strategies to effectively organise your study materials.

Gathering resources Collect all your textbooks, notes, and past papers for each subject. Organise digital resources into clearly labelled folders on your computer. Consider creating a ’study toolkit’ with essentials like highlighters, sticky notes, and index cards.

Creating a study-friendly environment Find a quiet, well-lit space where you can focus without distractions. Ensure you have a comfortable chair and desk at the right height. Keep your study area clean and organised – a tidy space can do wonders for your concentration.

t: Implement active recall and spaced repetition
b: Implement active recall and spaced repetition Below are some tried and true study techniques you might like to explore.

The power of self-testing After studying a topic, close your books and try to recall as much as you can. Create flashcards for key concepts and test yourself regularly. Explain concepts out loud as if you’re teaching someone else.
Spacing out your study sessions Avoid cramming by spreading out your study sessions over time. Review material at increasing intervals: e.g. 1 day later, 3 days later, 1 week later, etc.

t: Utilise practice exams and past papers
b: Utilise practice exams and past papers Another way to effectively prepare for exams is by practising past exams. Here are some techniques you might find helpful.

Simulating exam conditions Find past papers or practice exams for your subjects. Set up a quiet space and time yourself as you would in a real exam. Avoid using your notes or textbooks during these practice sessions.

Analysing your performance Mark your practice exams using the relevant marking schemes, if available. Identify areas where you lost marks and focus on improving these in your study sessions. Keep a log of common mistakes to avoid repeating them in the real exam.
Develop a healthy study-life balance It’s important to look after yourself and practice self-care during this time. Find what works best for you, or try our ideas below.

Incorporating breaks and relaxation Use techniques like the Pomodoro method: 25 minutes of focused study followed by a 5-minute break. Schedule longer breaks for activities you enjoy – maybe a quick game of basketball or a chat with friends. Practice mindfulness or meditation to help manage stress and improve focus.

Maintaining physical and mental well-being Aim for 7-9 hours of sleep per night – your brain consolidates memories and learning during sleep. Incorporate regular exercise to improve your mood and reduce stress. Eat a balanced diet with brain-boosting foods like blueberries, nuts, and fatty fish.
Collaborate with study groups Two heads are better than one, and a study group can be a powerhouse of knowledge, inspiration and motivation.

The benefits of peer learning Explaining concepts to others can help solidify your own understanding. Gain new perspectives and insights from your peers. Stay motivated and accountable with group study sessions.
Organising effective study sessions Set clear objectives for each study session. Use tools like shared Google Docs or virtual whiteboards for collaborative note-taking.
Seek help when needed Remember, asking for help isn’t a sign of weakness.
Utilising teacher support Don’t hesitate to approach your teachers with specific questions. Attend any extra help sessions offered by your school or community. Ask for feedback on your work.

Exploring additional resources Explore online tutorials or video explanations for challenging topics. Consider getting a tutor for subjects where you’re really struggling. Join online forums or study groups for your specific subjects.
Fine-tune your exam day strategy When your exams are approaching – make sure you’re feeling prepared.
Pre-exam preparation Get a good night’s sleep before the exam. Eat a nutritious breakfast to fuel your brain. Arrive at the exam venue early to avoid last-minute stress.

During the exam tactics Read through the entire paper before starting to answer questions. Manage your time wisely – allocate minutes to each section based on mark values. If you get stuck on a question, move on and come back to it later.

Study Tools Glossary of Techniques Every film and persuasive technique from the guide in one alphabetical reference. Ad hominem Metalanguage Attacking the person making an argument rather than the argument itself. Adjective Persuasive technique Describing words usually connected to a noun (naming word). e.g. The bright red house (bright and red = adjectives; house = noun) — Adds emphasis. Allegory Metalanguage A narrative whose characters and events stand for a parallel moral, political or historical meaning. Alliteration Persuasive technique Repeating and playing upon the same letter. e.g. A back-breaking job... — Adds emphasis and reinforces meaning, especially where an idea is repeated. Often used to create a highly emotive image. Allusion Metalanguage An indirect reference to another text, event or figure that imports its associations into the work. Anaphora Metalanguage Deliberate repetition of a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses to build rhythm and force. Anecdote Persuasive technique A short account or story of an entertaining or interesting incident. e.g. In my experience... — Usually makes reader sympathetic and receptive to the point; can set up a character, then position reader to accept or reject that individual character.
